{{Short description|American mathematician and computational linguist}}
{{Use mdy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=April 2021}}
{{Use list-defined references|date=April 2021}}
'''Joyce Barbara Friedman''' (1928 – November 28, 2018){{r|ww|obit}} was an American [[mathematician]], [[operations research]]er, [[computer scientist]], and [[computational linguistics|computational linguist]] who worked as a professor at the [[University of Michigan]] and [[Boston University]]{{r|ww}} and served as president of the [[Association for Computational Linguistics]].{{r|acl}}

==Early life and education==
Friedman was born in 1928. She was a Durant Scholar at [[Wellesley College]],{{r|durant}} from which she graduated in 1949, and earned a master's degree at [[Radcliffe College]] in 1952.{{r|ww}} In the same year she moved from the Logistics Research Project at [[George Washington University]] to the US Department of Defense,{{r|gwu}} later working at a succession of defense contractors: ACF Industries (where she worked with Sheldon Akers on [[Scheduling (production processes)|production scheduling]]),{{r|akers}} Tech. Operations, Inc., and the [[Mitre Corporation]].{{r|ww}}

Returning to graduate study at [[Harvard University]], her interests shifted from [[operations research]] to [[automated reasoning]]. She completed her Ph.D. in 1965, supervised by [[Hao Wang (academic)|Hao Wang]], with the dissertation ''A New Decision Procedure in Logic with a Computer Realization'',{{r|mg}} concerning computational methods in [[first-order logic]].{{r|andrews}}

==Academic career and later life==
Friedman worked as an assistant professor at [[Stanford University]] from 1965 until 1968, when she moved to the [[University of Michigan]] as an associate professor of computer and communications sciences. At Michigan, she was promoted to full professor in 1971. She moved to [[Boston University]] as chair of computer science in 1983.{{r|ww}}

Even before completing her doctorate, Friedman had worked at Mitre as a programmer for Donald E. Walker on a project for the US Air Force involving the development of programs that could answer English-language questions.{{r|mitre}}
As an academic, her research largely concentrated on [[computational linguistics]] and [[formal grammar]]s; she served as president of the [[Association for Computational Linguistics]] in 1971.{{r|acl}} Some of her work on [[transformational grammar]] was described in her 1971 book, ''A Computational Model of Transformational Grammar''.{{r|batori|bookrev}} She has over 180 [[academic genealogy|academic descendants]] through three of her doctoral students: [[C. Raymond Perrault]], [[Remko Scha]], and David S. Warren.{{r|mg}}

She died on November 28, 2018, in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]].{{r|obit}}

==Recognition==
Friedman was named a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1986.{{r|aaas}}
